In accordance with WAC 47563-100,-th e Appellant has filed exceptions to the Proposed
Decision issued on October 8, 2008, following a hearing conducted on October 2, 2008, by
Shirley J. Winsley, ViceC- hair, presiding officer for the Board ofTax Appeals (Board).
In order forthis Board to reconsider the decision set forth in the Proposed Decision, it
must be clear that thepresiding officer did not properly consider the evidence or that there was
an omission ofcertain pertinent facts or amisapplication ofthe law.
The Board reviewed the written exceptions, the Respondents' reply, the Proposed
Decision issued, and all available information and material. We conclude that the issues raised
by the Appellant were adequately addressed in the Proposed Decision, and that the evidence and
law wereproperly considered and applied. The Board finds no basis for changing the decision.
Therefore, we deny the exceptions and adopt the Proposed Decision as the Final Decision ofthis
Board.
I

courts have consistently addressed issues ofproperty assessments in that
manmer.35

In its sevensales ofraw land, GVA does not account for demolition costs of
structures on the site, site development and improvement costs, including
engineering, erosion control, landscaping, curbs, sidewalks, and utility costs.
None ofGVAs' seven sales have the superior DMU zoning ofthe subject. Five
ofthe sales border the Hilltop neighborhood ofTacoma (Sale Nos. 3,4 , 5, 6, and
7).T hese sale properties have a residential zoning. Yet, GVA finds these five

sale properties to be superior to the subject'slocation in downtown Tacoma,
which is within walking distance to the Courthouse, the Convention Center,
theaters, financial institutions, restaurants, and other Tacoma facilities..
GVA submits four land sales that took place in 2006. These four sales have a
lesser zoning than the subject and ranged from $23.94 to $40 per square foot.
The Assessor used a land value of 2$4.15 per square foot on the subject property
for assessment year 2006. Thus, the Board finds the Assessor's value ofthe
subject as an undeveloped site in 2006 was at the low-end ofthe sale-price range.
In comparison to twos-toryresidential townhouses proposed or constructed on the
sites ofSaleNos. 5, 6, and 7,t he subject is a six-story building withupper-floor
penthouses and underground parking. The Marcato advertises its location as a
vibrant urban village with panoramic views ofMt. Rainier, Commencement Bay,
the Tacoma Dome, Union Station, the Glass Museum, and the Tea Foss
Waterway. It boosts ofits gardens, plazas, and private- and publicg-athering
places.
GVA submits Exhibits 3 and 4 on how appraisers should value land. All ofthe
land appraisal theories presented in these exhibits do not address the issue before
the Board which is the market value ofeach individual unit ofthe Marcato
condos, ie..w, hat the units were selling for on the market in 2007. Most
appraisers are cognizantthat formore intensive land uses, such as central
business district multi-story office buildings, will generally result in a lower land
vtaoluet-taol-property value ratio.
GVA is critical ofthe Assessor's use ofthe cost approach in valuing the condo
units as new construction. GVAs' income approach concluded in a value of
2804,8950.,T he total sale price ofthe units sold (68 percent) is $14996,961,.
This is proof-that GVAs' income approach valuation is flawed.
The Assessor made the decision to uniformly apply the same land value to each
unit. As noted above, the Assessor is afforded considerable discretion to detennine the
methodology employed to arrive at market value. The Assessor admits that in the future,
after all units are sold, land values will bebased on the square footage ofeach unit,p lus a
percentage ratio ofthe underground parking, gardens, plazas, and the degree ofview
amenity ofeach unit. The land values will be higher formost units, not lower.
RCW 80460.08.prohibits this Board from raisingthe valuation ofaproperty to an
amount greater than the larger ofeither the valuation ofthe property by the assessor orthe
valuation oftheproperty assigned by the countyboard ofequalization. Ifthe Board were to
adjust the land value usingtheAssessor's total land valuation and GVA's proposal ofbasing
land value based on each units contributory pror-ata share ofbuilding area, itwould result
in a decreased land value for someunits and an increased landvalue on other units.
Likewise, to arrive at the fairmarketvalue ofeach unit, it would require ahigher
improvement value on some units and alowerimprovement value on other units.
What matters to the Owners ofthe subject property is a lower land assessment
value. They want the ability to market the condo units with emphasis ontheproperty-tax
exemption because the lower the land assessment ofeach unit, the lower the taxable
PROPOSED DECISION - Page 43 Docket No. 677096-7802

value ofeach unit. The Owners argue that the incentive ofthe propertyt- ax exemption
statute was to meet the residential property mandates ofthe GMA (Growth Management
Act).T he incentive to construct residential properties in downtown Tacoma will not be
met ifthe proper valuea-llocation is not attributed to the land.
The Board finds the legislative intent ofRCW 84.14 was to "increase and
improve residential opportunities, including affordable housing opportunities, within
these urban centers."T he legislature did not state that assessments should be based on
undeveloped land values. The Board finds that, an assessment value for tax purposes of
660,00 is realistic based on the total value ofthe subject units. The Board also notes
that several ofthe listed condo Owners purchased more than one unit. Thus, it concludes
that many units were purchased for investment purposes and the units are rented. There
was no testimony from the Owners that rents would decrease ifland values ranged from
7,319 to $330,80 per unit as recommended by GVA.
The letter from Mr. Teasley, Housing Division Manager for the City ofTacoma,
implies that not all oftheunits ofthe Marcato are eligible for the property-tax exemption
in 2007 for taxes due in 2008. He notes that the ten-year tax exemption will begin in
2007 on all residential units with a Temporary Certificate ofOccupancy; specifically, the
garage, and the first, fourth, and fifth floors. He notes that "any residential units which
are finalized later this year will begin receiving the tax exemption in 2008."
Since the letter is dated January 17, 2007, the Board concludes that Mr. Teasley
means assessment year 2008 for taxes due in 2009. Mr. Teasley specifically states: A" s
the legislation states, the property-tax exemption begins in the year following ?
completion."T herefore, since Mr. Teasley does not reference the second, third, and sixth
floors in his letter as having a Temporary Certificate ofOccupancy, these floors do not
qualify for an exemption in assessment year 2007 for taxes due in 2008. For the second,
third, and sixth floors, the property-tax exemption begins in 2008 for taxes due in 2009.
While the Owners argue over the land valuation, on their chart 38 it lists
improvement values that are considerably less than the purchase prices paid by buyers.
There is no need for the Owners to request areduction in the improvement values since
there is no tax for 10 years on improvements. Thus, their actions are unrealistic and
inconsistent with the purpose ofthe GVA appraisal and the Owners' marketing practices.
The Board finds that under University Village Ltd. Partners v. King County, it
matters not as to the value that the Assessor places on the land or the improvement as
long as the total value is within the fair market value as measured by market sales. The
Board notes that except for Condo UnitNo. 212, which sold for $3493, 61 in March 2007,
and is assessed at $354,600, the assessed value ofeach condo unit is less than the
purchase price. Thus, it is difficult to prove Assessor error.

ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS
Under the provisions ofRCW 8034041.( 0.)the,true and fair value ofproperty may be
based upon sales ofthe subject property or sales ofcomparable properties made within the past
five years. In addition, consideration maybe given to cost, cost less depreciation, and the
capitalization ofincome that would be derived from prudent use ofthe property. The Board
notes that RCW 804.340.02( )p rovides that, in the case ofthe subject property nothaving a
recorded sale within five years, and there notbeing a significant number ofsales ofsimilar
property in the area over the five-yearperiod, orin the case ofproperty ofa complex nature, cost
and capitalization ofincome maybe the dominant factors in valuation.
The valueplaced on the property by the Assessor is presumed to be correct, and can be
overcome only by presentation of c"lear, cogent and convincing"e vidence that the value is
erroneous.2 Clear, cogent, and convincing evidence means a quantum ofproofthat is less than
beyond areasonable doubt, but more than a mere preponderance ofthe evidence. It is the
quantum ofevidence necessary to convince the trier offact that the ultimate fact in issue is
highly probable3."
TheAssessors' arguments are supported inpart by sales thathave closing datesbeyond the
January 1,2 008, date ofassessment that applies here. Although there are no hard and fastrules
regardingtheuse ofsales that close afterthe assessment date, the Boardtends to apply adegree of
flexibilityinthe interest ofoptimizing themarketvalue guidelines that exist. The ideal is to have as
many comparable sales as possible that close on or around the assessment date. Traditionally, sales
priorto the assessment date aremost often used because, among other factors, there are normally
more ofthem. The Board frequently considers sales, however, that close afterthe January 1
assessment date ofa given assessment yearunder appeal. In this case, for example, sales with
closing dates inthemonths ofJanuary through June of2008 wouldtend tobe given equal weightin
the Board's decision process, other things being equal. Sales that closebeyond the firsthalfofthe
assessment year are given less and less weight as they approach the end oftheyear. At somepoint,

ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS
This Boards' goal in its hearings is to hear and weigh evidence to support a determination
oftrue and fair value as defined by statute 15 and the Washington Administrative Code. 1 6 Under
the provisions ofRCW 80434.00.and WAC 40583-007,-th e trueand fair value ofproperty shall
bebased upon sales ofthe subject property or sales ofcomparable properties made within the
past five years. The Assessor is afforded considerable discretion to determine the methodology
employed to arrive at market
value.7" "
Market value"m eans the amount ofmoney a willing
18
purchaser would pay to a willing seller.
The Assessor's valuation is presumed to be correct, and can be overcome only by
presentation of c"lear, cogent and convincing" evidence that the value is erroneous." Clear,
cogent, and convincing evidence means a quantum ofproofthat is less than beyond areasonable
doubt,b utmore than amere preponderance ofthe evidence. It is the quantum ofevidence
necessaryto convince the trier offact that the ultimate fact in issue is "highly probable.2" 0
The decision ofthe County Board is entitled to no evidentiary weightbefore this Board.
This hearing is considered de novo, or new.
Both parties present multiple sales. Neitherparty presents amap showing the location of
their sales or information showing specific features ofthe sales' properties such as view,
topography, etc. Neither party provides specific comparable sales from their sales or
adjustments ofthose sales to the subject parcels. The Owner does not provide expert appraisal
testimony, in fact no sworn testimony is provided at all. The Owner's evidence documents list
some sales viaREETAs, but the size ofthe sale properties is not provided. No market analysis
or value opinion is provided in the Owner's documents. The Assessor's testimony points out
that most ofthe Owner's sales are not fair market value transactions. The Owner provides only a
general value request ofbetween $30,00 to $60,00 per acre.
The Board finds the Owner fails to meet the burden ofproof. The Assessor notes that
most ofthe Owner's sales are not fair market value sales and should not be considered. The
Board agrees. The Owner provides no sworn testimony, sales analysis, or market comparisons:

ISSUES
The issues before the Board are the January 1, 2008,1 fair market values ofwhat was
originally an apartment complex, currently in the process ofbeing converted to condominium
ownership, located at 31420 106th Place SE in Auburn, Washington.
FACTS AND CONTENTIONS
Theunits to be analyzed are all contained within a development having relatively high
density aggregate physical characteristics. There are atotal of19 three- and twos-tory, wood-
frame structures built in 1982. The development has atotal of 132 units, o(nly 87 are under
appeal).T he total gross living areais 191,079 square feet. The averageunit size ofthe 132-unit
complex is approximately 14,48 square feet. There are three unit configurations: two-story
townhouse, three-story townhouse, and flats. The Assessor gives the subjectbuildings "average"
construction quality ratings; assigned condition ratings are "fair"a nd "average."P arking
accommodations include 222 parking spaces: 40 garage spaces, 73 carport spaces, and 109 open
spaces. The 454,7372 square foot (1a0c4.re4)-lo t is zoned R4,3 a zoning classification that
permits the current use. The overall site incurs topographic impacts ofa relatively undefined
nature.
Due to the condominium4 ownership status, each unit is assigned a separate parcel
number. In the hearing discussion that follows, they will be identified and addressed separately
by minors number for ease ofreference.

ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS
Undertheprovisions ofRCW 8034041.( 0.)the,true and fair value ofproperty may be
based upon sales ofthe subject property ando/ r sales ofcomparableproperties made within the
past fiveyears. In addition, consideration maybe given to cost, cost less depreciation, and the
capitalization ofincome that would be derived from prudentuse ofthe property. The Board
notes that RCW 80340(.420.)pro vides that, in the case ofthe subject property not having a
recorded sale within five years, and there not being a significant number ofsales ofsimilar
property in the area over the fivey-ear period, or in.the case ofproperty ofa complex nature, cost
and capitalization ofincomemay be the dominant factors in valuation.
The value placed on the property by the Assessor is presumed to be correct, and can be
overcome onlyby presentation of c"lear,c ogent and convincing"e vidence that the value is
erroneous.8 Clear, cogent, and convincing evidence means a quantum ofproofthat is less than
beyond areasonable doubt, but more than a mere preponderance ofthe evidence. It is the
quantum ofevidence necessary to convince the trier offact that the ultimate fact in issue is
highly probable.9"
The presumption ofcorrectness applies only to the Assessors' original value placed on
the property by the County Board. 1 0 When the Assessorrecommends a different value than that
originally assigned, theburden generally shifts to the preponderance ofthe evidence. The
taxpayer retains theburden
ofpersuasion.II
LEA's arguments are supported inpartbyan appraisal with effective dates ofFebruary 1,
2009, and April 1, 2009, and sales that have closing datesbeyond the January 1, 2008, date of
assessment that applies here. Although there arenohard and fastrulesregardingtheuse ofsales
that close afterthe assessment date, the Board tends to apply a degree offlexibility inthe interest of

possiblethat close onor around the assessment date. Traditionally, sales priorto the assessment

frequently considers sales, however, that close afterthe January 1 assessment date ofa given
assessment yearunder appeal. Inthis case, forexample, sales with closing dates inthe months of

January through July of2008 would tend to be given equal weight in the Board's decision process,
other things being equal. Although "the Board is not inclined to draw abright line cutting offthe
use ofsales at an express time period after the assessment date1,"2 sales that close beyond July of
the assessment year are given less and less weight as they approach the end ofthe year. At some
point, such evidencebecomes morerelevant for appeal arguments related to the following
assessment year.
Although thebeginning ofthe current recession has been back-dated to December 2007,
that was done afterthe fact, since there was no clear evidence at the time that there was a
recession, at least not in King County. In the general time period prior to the onset ofthe Great
Recession, there was even some discussion about the likelihood that the national recession would
bypass the Seattle area entirely. The Great Recession began in apublic, and national, sense with
the announcements ofthe failed banks in the late third quarter and the fourth quarter of2008.
The Board considers the late2-008 and early-2009 market environments to be entirely different
from that which prevailed on January 1, 2008.
The Board affirms the Assessor in these appeals because his arguments bestreflect the
market as it existed on July 31, 2008. LEA's appraisal and the associated values, although
disavowed by LEA in large part due to what it describes as the "inaccurate and unrealistic"
assumptions made in its production, are based on markets with effective dates in 2009. Although
LEA argues the February and April 2009 appraisal dates are essentially equal in market terms to
July 31, 2008, the Board finds this difficult to accept. More importantly, LEA provides
inadequate market support forthis argument.

ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION
RCW 82.04.080 authorizes the imposition of a Business and Occupation tax (B& O tax)
on gross income rather than net income. Hence, as a general rule, the base amount from which
the B& O tax is calculated does not allow for deductions for the expenses of conducting business.
Even though business expenses are generally not deductible, the Department ofRevenue has
adopted WAC 458-20- 111 ( Rule 111); Rule 111 recognizes that certain "pass through" expenses
should not be included in determining gross income. The Hospitals base their arguments under
the following three WAC provisions: 458-20- 111 ( Rule 111); 458-20- 159 ( Rule 159); and 458-
20- 199 ( Rule 199).
Rule 159. The Board' s analysis will not focus on Rule 159. The Department argues it is
for tangible properties. The Board agrees. Even a quick reading of the regulation supports this
conclusion. The Hospitals argue the Board should apply it by analogy, admitting the literal
language ofRule 159 speaks only about tangible properties. The Board declines to interpret the
rule by analogy when it is limited by its literal language to tangible properties.
Rule 199. The Board' s analysis will not focus on Rule 199. The Department argues the
rule is only about accounting methods and does not result in a deduction for the fees paid to the
emergency room physicians. The Board agrees. Additionally, the Department argues the
Hospitals did not raise this as a ground for their appeal; therefore, the Department did no
discovery on the accounting methods used. It is very difficult to understand how Rule 199 alone
would apply to. the Hospitals' factual situation and resultin a deduction. The Board finds Rule
199 does not provide a deduction for the Hospitals.
Rule 111. This Rule controls the outcome ofthese cases in the Board ofTax Appeals
opinion. Rule 111 is stated as follows:
WAC 458-20-111 Advances and reimbursements.
The word "advance" as used herein, means money or credits received by a taxpayer from
a customer or client with which the taxpayer is to pay costs or fees for the customer or
client.
FINAL DECISION - Page 5 Docket Nos. 01- 144, 01- 147 & 01- 149

The word " reimbursement" as used herein, means money or credits received from a
customer or client to repay the taxpayer for money or credits expended by the taxpayer in
payment of cost or fees for the client.
The words " advance" or "reimbursement" apply only when the customer or client alone is
liable for the payment of the fees or costs and when the taxpayer making the payment has no
personal liability therefor, either primarily or secondarily, other than as agent for the
customer or client.
There may be excluded from the measure of tax amounts representing money or credit
received by a taxpayer as reimbursement of an advance in accordance with the regular and
usual custom ofhis business or profession.
The foregoing is limited to cases wherein the taxpayer, as an incident to the business,
undertakes, on behalf of the customer, guest or client, the payment ofmoney, either upon an
obligation owing by the customer, guest or client to a third person, or in procuring a service
for the customer, guest or client which the does not or cannot render and for which no
liability attaches to the taxpayer. It does not apply to cases where the customer, guest or
client makes advances to the taxpayer upon services to be rendered by the taxpayer or upon
goods to be purchased by the taxpayer in carrying on the business in which the taxpayer
engages.
For example, where a taxpayer engaging in the business of selling automobiles at retail
collects from a customer, in addition to the purchase price, an amount sufficient to pay the
fees for automobile license, tax and registration of title, the amount so collected is not
properly a part of the gross sales ofthe taxpayer but is merely an advance and should be
excluded from gross proceeds of sales. Likewise, where an attorney pays filing fees or court
costs in any litigation, such fees and costs are paid as agent for the client and should be
excluded from the gross income of the attorney.
On the other hand, no charge which represents an advance payment on the purchase price
of an article or a cost of doing or obtaining business, even though such charge is made as a
separate item, will be construed as an advance or reimbursement. Money so received
constitutes a part of gross sales or gross income ofthe business, as the case may be. For
example, no exclusion is allowed with respect to amounts received by (1) a doctor for
furnishing medicine or drugs as a part ofhis treatment; (2) a dentist for furnishing gold,
silver or other property in conjunction with his services; ( 3) a garage for furnishing parts in
4) a manufacturer or contractor for materials purchased in his own
connection with repairs; (

vendor for the payment of the purchase price, regardless of whether the customer may also
be to there vendor for the payment ofthe purchase price; (5) any person engaging in a
service business or in the business of installing or repairing tangible personal property for
charges made separately for transportation or traveling expense.

By agreeing to pay a percentage ofthe gross billed amount, all three Hospitals fail to meet
the third prong set forth in Rule 111 and the case law interpreting it. The Hospitals are assuming
a business risk that payments from patients will exceed the amount paid to the ER physicians
after subtraction of hospital collection expenses. This assumption by the Hospitals makes the
Hospitals liable for the initial payments: Paying the ER physicians a percentage ofthe gross
amount billed is assuming a liability beyond that of an agent under the Christiansen test.
The Hospitals have no responsibility to make the payments on behalfofthe patient. The
Hospitals have no duty imposed by their relationship with patients to pay the emergency room
doctor. The Hospitals have voluntarily agreed to contract with and pay the ER physicians in
advance.
It is not the patients' expectation the Hospitals will pay their treating ER physician based
upon an affidavit submitted by the Hospitals. Common sense indicates this would not be the case
unless the patient is assuming the ER physicians are employees ofthe Hospitals: no doubt some
patients do make this assumption. There is no evidence presented showing patients are aware of,
or agree to, the practice of the three Hospitals. Under Rule 111, the key disqualifying factor is:
the Hospitals pay a set percentage ofthe billed amount, regardless ofwhether the patient actually
pays later. The Hospitals assume a business risk, similar to the risk an employer assumes when
paying its employees in advance; the assumption ofthis business risk is an action beyond the
scope of a pass-through agent.
None of the cases cited by the Hospitals where Rule 111 is applied, reflect facts where the
taxpayer pays regardless of later payment by the client/patient. In Christensen, supra, the

attorneys paid first via an advance; however, the client paid the actual amount later. In Medical

based upon the amount paid. The following cases denied Rule 111 application: William Rogers,
supra, the staffing agency functioned as an employer, paying regardless of client' s payment;
Pilcher, supra, Dr. Pilcher could pay his subcontracting physicians any rate he wanted to pay
regardless ofthe amount paid by the client.
The case law reflects the following theme: assume payment beyond a pass-through
agency relationship with the client and the business is liable for the B& O tax under Rule 111. By
guaranteeing payment of a percentage ofthe gross billings to the E R physicians, the Hospitals
are acting as more than a " pass through" agent. The " pass through" deduction, authorized by
Rule 111, does not extent to guaranteed payment ofthe gross amount billed by the ER
physicians. The Hospitals have assumed a business risk: Rule 111 does not exclude the money
paid to the. ER physicians by the Hospitals.

DISSENT
Gardner, Chair: I dissent in the analysis ofthe case law, in the application ofRule 111,
and in the decisions. In Docket No. 01- 144 (Northwest) and Docket No. 01- 149 (Holy Family),
the physicians who actually perform the emergency room services have contracted with a
separate and distinct entity, ESN and EPS, respectively. ESN and EPS contract with the
hospitals. In Docket No. 01- 147, the individual physicians contract with the hospitals. In all
FINAL DECISION - Page 13 Docket Nos. 01- 144, 01- 147 & 01- 149

three instances, the hospitals agree to provide collection services for a fee. In all three instances,
the hospitals account for and are held harmless from uncollectible amounts.
The first issue is the payment ofthe fee for the collection services provided. This is a
contractual requirement for all three hospitals. The hospitals have a right to retain a certain
percentage of monies collected to pay the prescribed fee. In some instances, the hospitals chose
not to be paid their full fees. Non-payment or underpayment does not alter the fact that the fees
are payable.
The second issue is the provision for uncollectible amounts. As prudent businesses, the
hospitals do not want to remit more than they have collected. They have therefore provided for a
means to determine uncollected or uncollectible amounts. There is no requirement that this
determination must be made on an invoice -by -invoice basis; there is no indication of any
preferred method for calculation ofuncollected amounts. Because ofthe sheer volume of
emergency room transactions, the individual charges become a fungible part of the whole.
Black' s Law Dictionary defines " fungible" as " regarded as commercially interchangeable with
other property of the same kind." 19 Just as it would be unreasonable to sort through a store of
apples to find the bad one, so is it unreasonable to expect the hospitals to track tens of thousands
of emergency room invoices individually. The hospitals, ESN, EPS, and the doctors (in the case
of Sacred Heart) have agreed to a methodology they find adequate to account for uncollectible
amounts.
The first prong of the Rule 111 test20 states the reimbursement of an advance may be
excluded if it is a part of the regular and usual custom of the business or profession. In the
timeline ofpayment for emergency room services, we know that a minority ofpatients pay cash
at the time of service. Some percentage ofpatients have insurance coverage, and those payments
come in after delay for processing claims. The balance ofthe charges incurred do not involve
third party reimbursement, and the hospitals are dependent on the ability and good will ofthe
patients for payment. In short, we know it is the usual custom ofthe hospital business to wait for
payment.
We also know it is the usual custom for suppliers to want payment. None ofus can
purchase goods or services, saying, " I' ll pay you when I get paid." We know we may have thirty
days, but we have to pay in a relatively timely fashion or we lose our ability to purchase. The
hospital has many employees who are paid semi-monthly or monthly regardless of collections.
The hospitals pay timely for laundry, supplies, and numerous other costs of doing business. We
stretch the bounds ofcommon sense ifwe contend the payment methodology by the hospitals
with regard to the subject contracts should be different.
The two service companies ( ESN and EPS) and the individual doctors at Sacred Heart
have entered into contracts with the hospitals that they will provide services to the hospital and
the hospital will provide collection services to them. The terms of the collection services are that
the hospitals will be paid for their services; that the hospitals will not be responsible for paying
19 Black' s Law Dictionary, Seventh Edition (1999), page 684.
20 Page 8, this decision.
FINAL DECISION - Page 14 Docket Nos. 01- 144, 01- 147 & 01- 149

the service companies or the doctors ( at Sacred Heart) for bills they can' t collect; and that the
transfers of funds will be made on a certain schedule.
The reimbursements made by the hospitals may be excluded if they are a part of the
regular and usual custom ofthe business. The first prong of the test is met. The assumptions of
the patients and whether there is an implied agency relationship do not defeat the simple
language ofRule 111.
The third prong ofRule 111 is that the taxpayer (the hospitals) is not liable for the
payment. The contracts between the parties are clear on this point: There will be a reduction in
remittances from the hospitals to reflect the accounts they couldn' t collect. The hospitals have
assumed no liability and that is all that Rule 111 asks.
A great deal of discussion is devoted to what the patients assume. Do patients assume
that the doctors are employed by the hospitals? Do patients assume the hospitals are responsible
for paying doctors under some form of contract? Do patients assume the doctor will personally
send them bills? The patients may wonder how they will pay the bill, but I suspect they don' t
give much thought to whose name is on the top. These questions do not bear on the matter before
the Board.
There is also much made of the fact that the hospitals sometimes " overpaid" ESN, EPS,
or the doctors (in the case of Sacred Heart) by failing to withhold sufficient funds to cover their
contractual collection fees. This is akin to a car dealership selling cars at cost or at a loss to
DARE programs or school drivers' education classes. There are many reasons a business may
not charge its " going rate" for their service or product. In may be inadvertent; it may be for
advertising; it may be for charity. It does not alter the question before us. Are the hospitals
liable to pay ESN, EPS, or the doctors (in the case of Sacred Heart) for amounts they cannot
collect on their behalf? The contracts say the hospitals are not so liable. The third prong ofRule
111 is met.

In Pilcher v. Dep' t of Revenue,`'' " the court held all the payments to Dr. Pilcher, both for
himself and the other physicians were taxable under the B& O tax." 24 Again, to paraphrase
substituting the Appellants in the case before us, we would conclude that all the payments to ESN
were taxable under the B& O tax. In Medical Consultants v. State,25 the " court
and EPS ...
indicated the third prong ofthe Christensen test was satisfied because Medical Consultants was
not obligated to pay the IME physicians unless it was first paid by its client. And our paraphrase
would be that ESN or EPS would not be obligated to pay the physicians unless it was first paid by
the hospitals.
By placing the names of ESN, EPS, or the hospitals in the corresponding position within
these cited decisions, it becomes clear that the decisions offer us little guidance in resolving the
issue presented to us. The question is summary judgment and we look to Rule 111 to direct the
decision. All members of this Board agree that the second prong of the Rule 111 test is met.
Because it is customary in the hospital business to pay contractual obligations when due rather
than when sufficient (or specific) funds have been collected to do so; because the collection agent
the hospitals) receive a fee for services rendered and bear no liability for uncollected amounts;
and because there is a reasonable method to account for uncollectible amounts, the first and third
prongs ofRule 111 have also been met.
It is my conclusion that summaryjudgment should be granted to Northwest Hospital
Center and denied to the Department ofRevenue (Docket No. 01- 144).
It is my conclusion that summaryjudgment should be granted to Sacred Heart Medical
Center and denied to the Department ofRevenue (Docket No. 01- 147.
It is my conclusion that summaryjudgment should be granted to Dominican Health
Services dba Holy Family Hospital and denied to the Department ofRevenue (Docket No. 01-

ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION
RCW 82.04.080 authorizes the imposition of a Business and Occupation tax (B& O tax)
on gross income rather than net income. Hence, as a general rule, the base amount from which
the B& O tax is calculated does not allow for deductions for the expenses of conducting business.
Even though business expenses are generally not deductible, the Department of Revenue has
adopted WAC 458-20- 111 ( Rule 111); Rule 111 recognizes that certain "pass through" expenses
should not be included in determining gross income. The Hospitals base their arguments under
the following three WAC provisions: 458-20- 111 ( Rule 111); 458-20-159 (Rule 159); and 458-
20- 199 (Rule 199).
Rule 159. The Board' s analysis will not focus on Rule 159. The Department argues it is
for tangible properties. The Board agrees. Even a quick reading ofthe regulation supports this
conclusion. The Hospitals argue the Board should apply it by analogy, admitting the literal
language ofRule 159 speaks only about tangible properties. The Board declines to interpret the
rule by analogy when it is limited by its literal language to tangible properties.
Rule 199. The Board' s analysis will not focus on Rule 199. The Department argues the
rule is only about accounting methods and does not result in a deduction for the fees paid to the
emergency room physicians. The Board agrees. Additionally, the Department argues the
Hospitals did not raise this as a ground for their appeal; therefore, the Department did no
discovery on the accounting methods used. It is very difficult to understand how Rule 199 alone
would apply to the Hospitals' factual situation and result in a deduction. The Board finds Rule
199 does not provide a deduction for the Hospitals.
Rule 111. This Rule controls the outcome ofthese cases in the Board ofTax Appeals
opinion. Rule 111 is stated as follows:
WAC 458-20-111 Advances and reimbursements.
The word "advance" as used herein, means money or credits received by a taxpayer from
a customer or client with which the taxpayer is to pay costs or fees for the customer or
client.

The word "reimbursement" as used herein, means money or credits received from a
customer or client to repay the taxpayer for money or credits expended by the taxpayer in
payment of cost or fees for the client.
The words " advance" or "reimbursement" apply only when the customer or client alone is
liable for the payment of the fees or costs and when the taxpayer making the payment has no
personal liability therefor, either primarily or secondarily, other than as agent for the
customer or client.
There may be excluded from the measure oftax amounts representing money or credit
received by a taxpayer as reimbursement of an advance in accordance with the regular and
usual custom of his business or profession.
The foregoing is limited to cases wherein the taxpayer, as an incident to the business,
undertakes, on behalfof the customer, guest or client, the payment ofmoney, either upon an
obligation owing by the customer, guest or client to a third person, or in procuring a service
for the customer, guest or client which the does not or cannot render and for which no
liability attaches to the taxpayer. It does not apply to cases where the customer, guest or
client makes advances to the taxpayer upon services to be rendered by the taxpayer or upon
goods to be purchased by the taxpayer in carrying on the business in which the taxpayer
engages.
For example, where a taxpayer engaging in the business of selling automobiles at retail
collects from a customer, in addition to the purchase price, an amount sufficient to pay the
fees for automobile license, tax and 'registration of title, the amount so collected is not
properly a part ofthe gross sales ofthe taxpayer but is merely an advance and should be
excluded from gross proceeds of sales. Likewise, where an attorney pays filing fees or court
costs in any litigation, such fees and costs are paid as agent for the client and should be
excluded from the gross income of the attorney.
On the other hand, no charge which represents an advance payment on the purchase price
of an article or a cost of doing or obtaining business, even though such charge is made as a
separate item, will be construed as an advance or reimbursement. Money so received
constitutes a part of gross sales or gross income of the business, as the case may be. For
example, no exclusion is allowed with respect to amounts received by (1) a doctor for
furnishing medicine or drugs as a part of his treatment; (2) a dentist for furnishing gold,

Black' s Law Dictionary defines " fungible" as " regarded as commercially interchangeable with
other property of the same kind.i19 Just as it would be unreasonable to sort through a store of
apples to find the bad one, so is it unreasonable to expect the hospitals to track tens ofthousands
of emergency room invoices individually. The hospitals, ESN, EPS, and the doctors (in the case
of Sacred Heart) have agreed to a methodology they find adequate to account for uncollectible
amounts.
The first prong ofthe Rule 111 test20 states the reimbursement ofan advance may be
excluded if it is a part of the regular and usual custom ofthe business or profession. In the
timeline ofpayment for emergency room services, we know that a minority of patients pay cash
at the time of service. Some percentage ofpatients have insurance coverage, and those payments
come in after delay for processing claims. The balance ofthe charges incurred do not involve
third party reimbursement, and the hospitals are dependent on the ability and good will ofthe
patients for payment. In short, we know it is the usual custom ofthe hospital business to wait for
payment.
We also know it is the usual custom for suppliers to want payment. None ofus can
purchase goods or services, saying, " I' ll pay you when I get paid." We know we may have thirty
days, but we have to pay in a relatively timely fashion or we lose our ability to purchase. The
hospital has many employees who are paid semi-monthly or monthly regardless of collections.
The hospitals pay timely for laundry, supplies, and numerous other costs of doing business. We
stretch the bounds of common sense ifwe contend the payment methodology by the hospitals
with regard to the subject contracts should be different.
The two service companies (ESN and EPS) and the individual doctors at Sacred Heart
have entered into contracts with the hospitals that they will provide services to the hospital and
the hospital will provide collection services to them. The terms of the collection services are that
the hospitals will be paid for their services; that the hospitals will not be responsible for paying

the service companies or the doctors (at Sacred Heart) for bills they can' t collect; and that the
transfers of funds will be made on a certain schedule.
The reimbursements made by the hospitals may be excluded ifthey are a part of the
regular and usual custom ofthe business. The first prong of the test is met. The assumptions of
the patients and whether there is an implied agency relationship do not defeat the simple
language ofRule 111.
The third prong of Rule 111 is that the taxpayer (the hospitals) is not liable for the
payment. The contracts between the parties are clear on this point: There will be a reduction in
remittances from the hospitals to reflect the accounts they couldn' t collect. The hospitals have
assumed no liability and that is all that Rule 111 asks.
A great deal of discussion is devoted to what the patients assume. Do patients assume
that the doctors are employed by the hospitals? Do patients assume the hospitals are responsible
for paying doctors under some form ofcontract? Do patients assume the doctor will personally
send them bills? The patients may wonder how they will pay the bill, but I suspect they don' t
give much thought to whose name is on the top. These questions do not bear on the matter before
the Board.
There is also much made ofthe fact that the hospitals sometimes " overpaid" ESN, EPS,
or the doctors (in the case of Sacred Heart) by failing to withhold sufficient funds to cover their
contractual collection fees. This is akin to a car dealership selling cars at cost or at a loss to
DARE programs or school drivers' education classes. There are many reasons a business may
not charge its " going rate" for their service or product. In may be inadvertent; it may be for
advertising; it may be for charity. It does not alter the question before us. Are the hospitals
liable to pay ESN, EPS, or the doctors (in the case of Sacred Heart) for amounts they cannot
collect on their behalf? The contracts say the hospitals are not so liable. The third prong ofRule
111 is met.

This appeal 1s one of a large number of appeals, all pertaining to the value
of land with no appeals being made with respect to any improvements located thereon.
Formal appeals, Docket Numbers 69-9 through 69- 40 and 69- 53 and 69- 54 were filed and
heard on behalf of the property owners as appellants. Informal appeals, Docket
Numbers 456 through 510, 512, 617 and 618 were filed and heard on behalf of Allen 8.
Morgan, Assessor. Ring County. With the exception of Docket Numbers 500 and 512,
each formal Docket Number has as a cross-appeal one or more informal Docket Numbers
involving collectively the sage land under appeal.
All of these appeals, including Docket Numbers 500 and 512 were consolidated
for the purpose of being heard in one bearing. At the bearing each appeal was
separately identified and testified to before the Board. Again, for the purposes of
the haring, the property owners and the assessor, agreed by stipulation of counsel
that the testimony and evidence submitted with respect to each appeal and parcel of
property would be applicable and incorporated by reference to both the formal and
the informal appeals concerned. The purpose of the stipulation being to avoid a
duplication and a repetitious production of all the evidence involved.
The assessor in presenting recant sales of comparable properties in the area
generally denominated the Enemclaw Bench area) and comparing and relating them to
specific properties under appeal has, with a substantial preponderance of such
detailed and specific evidence, overcome the ruling of the July 1969 Ring County
Board of Equalisation requiring a horizontal reduction of 112 applicable to all the
properties under appeal.
ECU 84. 40.030 states:
A11 property shall be assessed fifty percent of its true and fair
value in money. In determining the true and fair value of real or
personal property, the assessor shall not adopt a lower or different
standard of value because the same is to serve as a basis of taxation;
nor shall he adopt as a criterion of value the price for which the
said property would sell at auction, or at a forced sale, or in the
aggregate with all the property in the town or district; but he shall
value each article or description of property by itself, and at such
price as he believes the same to be fairly worth in mosey at the time.
such ssent is made."
The Washington State Supreme Court referring to this matter in Mason County
Overtaxed, Inc. v. Maaon County 62 Wn. 2d. 677 ( 1963) stated in its syllabus:
The provision of BCW 84. 40. 030 which directs an assessor to base
his anent of property on the ' true and fair value in money'
means that the assessment shall be basad upon market value, 1. e.,
the amount of money a purchaser, willing but not obligated to buy,
would pay an owner willing, but not obligated to sell, and the
sentimental value to, or the personal evaluation by, the owners
are no part of this valuation."

PAGE 2
ADDENDUM
We find from the evidence the various properties had sufficient individual
characteristics to indicate they required and should have had an individual
appraisal approach made to each property. This Board, therefore, finds the 112
horizontal reduction, as applied to the values of all the properties under appeal,
was improper and not reflective of the true and fair market value of these properties.
As a result thereof, this lard in considering comparative sales of properties
in an effort to establish the true and fair market values of the subject properties,
finds the only indication of valuations as required by WAC 456-08- 620 produced by
the appealing property owners vas, in fact, a class contention relating to all of
the, namely, that the correct values were the values placed upon the properties
by the assessor for the year preceding the year under appeal. We find the property
owners introduced no affirmative evidence, by way of sales of comparable properties
or other indications of value of • positive nature, which this Board could use as
a basis of valuation. During the course of the hearing a continuing approach was
made upon cross-examination directed to the credibility of the assessor' s assessment
and techniques, but this again produced no affirmative evidence upon which this
Board could predicate any significant impeachment of the assessor' s testimony,
evidence or appraisal techniques. This produced no evidence upon which a value
different from the value produced by the assessor could be reasonably based.
Om the other hand, from an examination of 500 sales in the ares, the assessor
found 101 to be comparable to properties involved in these appeals. The assessor
presented direct testimony as to some of these comparable sales and related them
to specific properties involvd in these appeals. Pursuant to a stipulation of
the parties this became au evidentiary part of both the formal and the informal
appeals. The assessor stated that he personally inspected most but not all of the
comparable properties.
Where improvements were present on the properties being compared, the appealing
property owners challenged the values placed upon the improvements by the assessor
for the purpose of extracting such value from the total property value to determine
the resulting land value. The challenge were made that the assessor' s calculations
were not accurate. Despite reputed requests by the Board, both before and at the
hearing, no rebuttal evidence was introduced by the property owners to show or
establish a specific value for the extracted improvements different from the value
set by the assessor.
From the evidence presented, it has become clear the assessor in making his
property appraisals has found differences in acreage values. The physical differences
found by the assessor have been reflected in the varying appraised values he has set.
It is clear the asssssor has not used an across-the-board or class appraisal approach
to the valuation of the entire Enumclaw Bench are*.
The assessor' s counsel developed through his witnesses the characteristics of
each subject property to a degree and in such manner that this Board was made
of the availability or non-availability of piped water and whether it was limited
in quantity, such as a 2 -inch main or up to and including an 8 -inch main and their
relative values. He developed characteristics with respect to road frontages and
topographical features, wen to the extent of pointing out the properties above or
below road level where road frontages were involved. Further, he developed additional
factors, such as characteristics of view, and the general water or drainage problems
of each property. He indicated such drainage problems were typical of much of the
entire Enumclaw beach area within which the appealed properties are situated.

PACE 3
In evaluating the sales of comparable Lads used by the assessor the Board
notes We application of a rather definitive appraisal technique. Per example,
is attributing a value to more than one road frontage adjoining a particular
tract the assessor frequently applied a different valuation to each road frontage
in recognition of its different asset value to the property being valued.
Macy of the comparative lamas have higher market values then the lands of the
taxpayers in these appeals and the assessor pointed this out in relating the sales
of these comparable lands to the lands under appeal.
The Board hes taken note some of the property owners in these appeals bare
in a fa instances introduced evidence relative to income received from their
dairy farms. The neo -detailed evidence, however, failed to establish a full true
and fair market value of the property measured by or based upon the evidence of
income. The evidence is such cases did establish, however, that the operation of
dairy farms could not be considered a proper measure of the full true and fair market
values of the lads concerned. The theoretical evidence reflected a value very such
below current prices being paid for comparable lands in the area. The values
reflected by income from dairy farming proceeds were much below prices for lad
being purchased or sold in soma cases by the appealing property owners themselves.
That dairy farming in the Enumclaw bench area is declining was brought o,,.
clearly by the property wears' witness, Nr. Harbert Sorensen. who testified as to
the transitional nature of the area subsequent to 1964. Mr. Sorensen testified that
historically the dairy farmer who put out cans of milk daily for pickup is gone.
It. Sorensen9 oho hes been engaged la the business of selling real estate in this
area over a period of years beginning such before 1964 and continuing to the present,
also testified that inertias in 1964 a sudden influx of people were buying smaller
acreages of. 20 to 60 acres for hams sites and were daily commuting to work in the
Seattle area. lt. Sorensen indicated this transition is still continuing.
As indicated above, the property owners in these appeals have not presented
affirmative evidence to establish and support the lad values they have conteded
for. They love attacked the credibility of the evidence presented by the assessor,
but the assessor has at great length and 1n specific detail affirmatively established
his basis for the values he has set and with vary extensive evidence has substantiated
such values. The Board finds that the valuations made by the assessor appear to be
proper in terms of the extensive testimony which hes been presented in these appeals
and therefore affirms these values.
This Board is of the opinion its decisions in these appeals are well founded.

The issue in this appeal is the January I, 1995, true and fair

improvement with garage and basement located on this parcel of

Owner contends that the total property value, in his opinion, is

In determining the value of this appeal, the Owner has relied
on relating to assessed values of other properties as compared to
the assessed value of the subject. The Owner introduced one sale
indicating a sale price of $ 145, 000 and noted that the assessment
on this property is $158, 610. He stated this property is located
1, 140 feet from the subject property. The Owner argued the
comparable sales used by the Assessor are not reliable indicators
of value because of many varying reasons. He stated that sales
activity within the area of the subject is stagnant. He agreed
that many properties in the area are better than the subject but
noted, from his observation, they are assessed similar to the

improvement was self constructed some 17 years ago. He said the
roof of the improvement needs some repair and other repairs are
needed. He also stated the current assessment of $58. 99 per square
foot, as determined by the Assessor, is high when compared to other
assessments in the area.

the Owner provided the following:
Washington Constitution Art 7, Sec. 1 ( amendment 14)
All taxes shall be uniform upon the same class of
property within the territorial limits of the authority
levying the tax .

plain for argument that to pick out the property of a
particular owner and raise the assessed valuation of his

sales indicate an average price per acre of $ 7, 750. The Assessor
stated that the short-platted land is assessed at $ 6, 500 per acre

sales were not received in a timely manner. They were received by

The Assessor is required to establish the true and fair value
of residential property based upon sales of the subject property or
sales of comparable properties made within the past five years.
RCW 84. 40. 030. True and fair value is "market value", that is, the
price to be paid by a willing buyer to a willing seller. Carkon~n
v_ Williams, 76 Wn. 2d 617, 458 P. 2d 280 ( 1969).
Under RCW 84. 40. 0301, the valuation placed on property by the
Assessor is presumed to be correct, and can only be overcome upon
presentation by the taxpayer of clear, cogent, and convincing
evidence that the assessor' s valuation of the subject property is
erroneous. IIClear, cogent and convincing" evidence means a quantum
of proof which is less than beyond a reasonable doubt, but more
than a mere preponderance of the evidence. It is the quantum of
evidence necessary to convince the trier of fact that the ultimate
fact in issue is " highly probable". In re g~aq, 82 Wn. 2d 736, 513
P. 2d 831 ( 1973).
The sales comparison approach is based on the premise that
the market value of a property is directly related to the prices of
comparable, competitive properties. The value of a property in the
market is set by the availability of substitute properties of
similar utility and desirability." Appraisal Institute, . IM.
AnnraiAal of Rp.~l ERtatp. 403 ( 10th ed. 1992)
In our review of the comparable sales provided, this Board
gives the most weight to those sales located nearest to the
subject, judged to be most similar, occurring closest to the
January 1, 1994 valuation date in question. After reviewing those
sales presented, we find those sales presented by the Assessor to
be similar in location, and comparable in age, style and quality of
construction. Considering the range in value from $ 270, 000 to
282, 500, we find the total value of the subject as determined by
the Assessor to be well supported.
Although the arguments made on behalf of the Owners are
interesting and persuasive, they lack documentation. RCW
84. 40. 0301 (1) clearly states that the burden is on those who
challenge the Assessor' s valuation. Although the Owners provided
some information regarding comparable sales, this Board requires
specific information regarding those sales and their comparability
to the subject. Without specific market evidence, this Board has
no alternative other than to find that the Owner has not presented
the clear, cogent and convincing evidence necessary to overcome the
presumption of correctness of the value established by the
Assessor.

ANAT,VSTS AND CONCLTTSTONS
This BoardIs goal in its hearings is the acquisition of
sufficient, accurate evidence to support a determination of true
and fair value as defined by statute ( RCW 84. 40. 030) and the
Washington Administrative Code ( WAC 458- 12- 301).
The valuation placed on the property by the assessor is
presumed to be correct, and can only be overcome by presentation of
clear, cogent, and convincing evidence that the value is erroneous.
RCW 84. 40. 0301; Weverhaeuspr roo v. Eastp~, 126 Wn. 2d 370, 894 P. 2d
1290 ( 1995). " Clear, cogent, and convincing" evidence means a
quantum of proof which is less than beyond a reasonable doubt, but
more than a mere preponderance of the evidence. It is the quantum
of evidence necessary to convince the trier of fact that the
ultimate fact in issue is " highly probable". In re SeaD, 82 Wn. 2d
736, 513 P. 2d 831 ( 1973).
When available, comparable sales are the preferred evidence of
value. Comparable sales closest to the lien date are given the
most weight.
Market value is best derived from the analysis of sales of
similar properties. Income and cost approaches will only be given
substantial weight in the absence of adequate market data.
This Board has carefully reviewed the arguments set forth in
the Owners' petition and has considered the evidence entered into
the record by the Assessor. For ad valorem tax purposes real
property must be assessed at 100 percent of its indicated true and
fair value. We find that, from the analysis of the sales
introduced by the Assessor, the current assessment of the subject
property does not exceed its true and fair value.

This Board finds that the Owners have not presented the clear,
cogent, and convincing evidence necessary to overcome the
presumptive correctness of the value established by the Assessor.
We, therefore, sustain the value established by the Assessor.

ISSUES
The issues in these appeals are the true and fair values of
land and improvements identified as Parcel No. 272601- 1- 008- 2004.
The property is described as a single- family residence, one and
one- half 3tory, with a full basement and an attached double garage.
The residence is situated on a parcel of land containing . 81 acre.

FACT~ AND CONTENTIONS
The Owner' s arguments, set forth in Exhibit A- I, primarily
relate to his contended inability to meet the increases in property
tax assessments. This, he stated, is because he is retired and on
a fixed income.
The Owner stated that in searching for sales of similar

office failed to disclose any comparable sales. The subject:.
residence was originally built in ~9S4 and remodeled in 1980. The
Assessor' s 25 percent depreciation factor is, in his opinion,
inadequate for a home which is 43 years old. He contended that the
comparable sales used by the Assessor are not similar to the
subject and do not serve to fairly indicate the value of the
subject property. Further, conditions which he contends would
affect the value are its location on Liberty Bay which, he says, is
one of the most polluted bodies of water in the Puget Sound area.
The Assessor testified that the value of the subject property
had been determined by the market data approach. The Assessor
stated that her office is very concerned about the increasing
values and makes extensive efforts to value all properties
according to the value as indicated in the marketplace and as
required by Washington statutes.
The Assessor stated the valuation of this property changed in
1994 for taxes payable in 1995 under the Kitsap County Assessor' s
Cyclical Revalll-3tion Program. The Assessor said, at the Owner' s
request, a reexamination was made of the property on October 13,
1993, with the Owner present and a complete verification of all
property characteristics was made.
To support the current assessed value, the Assessor introduced
three sales for this Board' s consideration. These sales, in their
brief form, are as follows:
Sale No. 1 is a property located near the subject and
similar in most respects. This sale indicated a value of
235, 000 and was consummated in Februa;~ 1994. The land
is . 50 acre with 50 waterfront feet. The improvement was
constructed in 1922 and is a one and one- half story

Sale No. 2 is a single- family residence which sold for

ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS
The Assessor is required to establish the true and fair value
of property based upon sales of the subject property or sales of
comparable properties made within the past five years. RCW
84. 40. 030. True and fair value is " market value". that is. the
price to be paid by a willing buyer to a willing seller. Carkonen
v. William~, 76 Wn. 2d 617, 458 P. 2d 280 ( 1969).
Accrued depreciation is the difference between the
reproduction or replacement cost of the improvements on the
effective date of the appraisal and the market value of the
improvements on the same date. Depreciation is caused by
deterioration or obsolescence in the property. Deterioration is
evidenced by wear and tear on the structure. Functional
obsolescence is caused by internal property characteristics such as
a poor floor plan, inadequate mechanical equipment, or functional
inadequacy or superadequacy due to size or other characteristics.
External obsolescence is caused by conditions outside the property
such as a lack of demand. Changing property uses in the area, or
national economic conditions. Some types of depreciation interact
with one another and the analysis of depreciation from all causes
is cumulative. Appraisal Institute. Thp Annrai~al of Real F.~tate
320 ( 10th ed. 1992).
The value of property for purposes of ad valorem taxation is
Umarket value", that is: " the amount of money which a purchaser
willing, but not obligated, to buy would pay an owner willing, but
not obligated, to sell, taking into consideration all uses to which
the property is adapted and might in reason be applied." Mason

P. 2d 352 ( 1963); accord, Carknn~n v. Williams, 76 Wn. 2d 617, 458
P. 2d 280 ( 1969).
In the evaluation of the evidence, as presented by the Owner,
this Board finds no conclusive evidence which would relate
specifically to the true and fair value of the subject of this
appeal.
The Assessor has met the mandate of the Washington statutes by
relating sales of similar properties and adjusting those sales to
best reflect the value of the subject property as of the assessment
date. The Assessor provided adequate data relating to each of the
sales which she considered so that this Board may make a complete
review of the sales and determine the reliability of the evidence.
We find the evidence presented by the Assessor to
substantially support the values of both land and improvements as
set forth in the Kitsap County Board of Equalization orders for
each assessment year.
pECISTON
In Docket Nos. 48324 and 49061, the Owner' s petition is
denied. The values for land and improvements, as determined by the
Kitsap County Board of Equalization, are affirmed.
The Kitsap County Assessor and Treasurer are hereby directed
that the assessment and tax rolls of Kitsap County are to accord
with and give full effect to the provisions of this decision.

ISSUE
The issue in this appeal is the January 1, 1994, true and fair
value of the Seafirst bank property located at 301 NE Northgate
Way, Seattle, Washington. The Assessor valued the subject property
at $ 1, 743, 300, which was sustained by the Board of Equalization.
Seafirst appealed to this Board contending a value of $1, 345, 000.
FACTS AND CONTENTIONS
The subject property is located within the Northgate Mall, at
the far north end. The property consists of a separate pad type
parcel, 9, 367 square feet in size. The parcel has a " NC385/1'
commercial zoning classification. Improvements consist of a one-
story, masonry, branch bank building, built in 1951. The building,
which includes a 8, 906 square foot unfinished basement, has a first
floor rentable area of 8, 956 square feet. The Assessor lists the

building as good in construction quality and states the bank is a
modern looking facility due to various renovations.
Seafirst explained that although the subject is located within
the Northgate Malll a long corridor separates the bank from the
main mall. Also, this branch bank has no drive-up banking
facilities, and drive-up banking is not possible at this location.
To support its contended value, Seafirst relied on the sales
comparison approach. Seafirst provided ten branch bank sales.
Seafirst reviewed these sales, noting Sales Nos. 1 and 7 are given
little weight due to the less than arm' B length nature of the
transactions, Sale No. 2 has excess land, and Sale No. 3 has a
corner pad Southcenter Mall location. These ten properties sold
between September 1992 and March 1995, reflecting price per square
foot of building area indications ranging from $103. 44 to $189. 05.
Based on these sales, Seafirst concludes a value of $150 per square
foot is indicated for the subject, resulting in a value of
1, 345, 000.
Seafirst also provided data on eight recently negotiated
branch bank leases. These leases reflect annual lease rates
ranging from $ 10 to $ 20. 42 per square foot. Seafirst did not
include an income analysis of the subject, stating these leases
were provided as back-up information.
The Assessor explained he valued the subject as a portion of
the Northgate Mall economic unit. He described the subject as
having a good location at the north end of the mall and that the
subject could easily be remodeled into retail space.
The Assessor provided his original appraisal of the entire
mall, which includes three spreadsheets showing the various
portions of the mall and their values. He stated the cost and
income approaches were used, with most weight given to the income
approach. The Assessor stated the subject' s assessed value was
based on an economic lease rate of $24. 00 per square foot and an
8. 75 percent overall capitalization rate. To support his economic
lease rate, the AsseSBor cited a $ 22 per square foot branch bank
lease ( which he adjusted upward for the subject' s mall location)
and stated the going retail lease rate range in the mall is $22 to
24 per square foot.
The Assessor also included three comparable sales. These
sales reflect price per square foot of rentable area indications
ranging from $173. 41 to $235. 02. The Assessor believes these sales
have inferior locations, and noted it is difficult to find "clean"
bank sales due to the numerous bank mergers and resulting swapping
of assets. The Assessor concludes both the income and market
approaches support his assessed value at $194. 65 per square foot of
building area.

In response to Seafirst' s arguments and evidence, the Assessor
stated: 1) if the subject was a detached bank branch, he would not
have used an 8. 75 percent overall rate; and 2) because it is
connected to the mall, the Assessor contends it is appropriate to
value the subject as part of the mall.
In rebuttal, Seafirst stated: 1) it was unable to reach the
subject' s specific assessed value from the Assessor' s total mall
analysis; 2) Seafirst contends the lease rate for its Lake Forest
Park branch is $15 per square foot, not the $ 22 per square foot
amount cited by the Assessor; 3) compared to the other branch bank
comparables, the subject has no drive-up banking facilities and
Seafirst developed a separate drive-up facility across the street,
valued at $600, 000; and 4) the subject is not retail space now and
conversion would require renovation costs.
ANALYSTS AND CONCT,tJSIONS
This Board, giving full opportunity for all arguments and
having considered all testimony and documentary evidence submitted
by the parties in support of their respective positions, hereby
enters the following analysis and conclusions:
Under the provisions of RCW 84. 40. 030 and WAC 458- 12- 301, the
true and fair value of property shall be based upon sales of the
subject property or sales of comparable properties made within the
past five years. In addition, consideration may be given to cost,
cost less depreciation, and the capitalization of income that would
be derived from prudent use of the property. True and fair value
is "market value," that is, the price to be paid by a willing buyer
to a willing seller. ~ arkonen v. William~, 76 Wn. 2d 617, 458 P. 2d
280 ( 1969).
The valuation placed on the property by the Assessor is
presumed to be correct, and can only be overcome by presentation of
clear, cogent and convincing evidence that the value is erroneous.
RCW 84. 40. 0301( 1).
The Assessor primarily relied on an income analysis of the
entire mall to support his contended value for the subject. This
Board understands the mass appraisal nature of the Assessor' s work
and the reasons for including the subject within this overall mall
analysis. However, like Seafirst, we t.oo had a difficult time
equating this overall analysis to a specific value for the subject.
Another problem is the issue of land value contributions within
this overall mall analysis, especially considering the subject' s
small ( pad) land size. This issue was not addressed. Also,
although the Assessor discussed economic lease rates in general, no
specific data regarding these properties was provided ( such as
size, location, etc.) to enable effective consideration. Seafirst
PROPOSED DECISION - Page 3 Docket No. 48325

did not provide an income analysis, but did submit actual branch
bank lease data for consideration.
After review of the information provided, we believe the sales
submitted by the parties provide the best market evidence. Of the
sales provided, most weight is given to Assessor' s Sale No. 3 and
Seafirst' s Sales Nos. 3 and 4. Two of these sales are located
close to the subject on NE Northgate Way, and the other is adjacent
to Southcenter Mall. These sales reflect price per square foot of
rentable area indications of $173, $ 158 and $ 146. While we agree
with the Assessor' s position that the subject' s location within the
mall is a plus, the subject' s lack of drive-up banking facilities
should also be considered. Overall, we conclude the market
evidence supports a value of $1, 522, 500 for the subject -- $ 170. 00
per square foot.
DECISION
The decision of the Board of Equalization is set aside. Based
on the evidence provided, this Board finds that the true and fair
value of the Subject property, as of January 1, 1994, is
1, 522, 500, as set forth on page one of this decision.
The King County Assessor is hereby directed that the
assessment and tax rolls of King County are to accord with and give
full effect to the provisions of this decision.

ISSUE
The issue in this appeal is the July 31, 2018,2 true and fair market value of residential
property located at 9114 NE 32nd Street, Yarrow Point, Washington.
PROCEDURAL HISTORY
The Assessor initially assigned the subject property a value of $1,343,000, which
represented a land value of $647,999 and an improvement value of $696,000; however, in
reviewing the materials for the original appeal to the King County Board of Equalization
(County Board), the Assessor recalculated the improvement from 44 percent complete to 28
percent complete as of July 31, 2018. This was a manifest error correction.3 The Owners
appealed the original valuation to the County Board, which sustained the Assessor’s revised
value. The Owners now appeal to this Board, contending the value above. The Assessor asks
the Board to sustain the revised value.
FACTS AND CONTENTIONS
In 2018, the subject property was being improved with grade-9,4 single-family residence
on a 9,430-square-foot lot. The Assessor codes the property for extreme traffic nuisance.
Owners’ Evidence and Arguments
In support of a reduced value, the Owners explain that their property is one of the
smallest lots on their street, but its assessed value is one of the highest in the neighborhood. On
a per-square-foot basis, their lot has the highest valuation in the neighborhood.
The Owners explain that the zoning in their area is R-15,5 and so larger lots can be
subdivided and further developed. The Yarrow Point development code specifies that homes
cannot exceed 30 percent lot coverage, and so larger homes can be built on larger lots, making

31st of each year. The assessed valuation of the property shall be considered as of July 31st of that year.”

good; grade 9, better; grade 10, very good; grade 11, excellent; grade 12, luxury; and grade 13, mansion; grade 13+99,
mansion+; and grade 20, exceptional.
5 R-15 requires a building lot size of 15,000 square feet. Yarrow Point Municipal Code 17.16.010(b).

the larger lots more desirable and salable. This meant that they were required to build a two-

traffic noise upstairs is much, much worse. The Owners note that the Assessor has noted the

The Owners note that land values in the neighborhood were increased for 2019, and that

The Assessor notes that the comparison of assessed valuations is not a valid appraisal

PROPOSED DECISION - Page 5 Docket No. 96291

APPLICABLE LAW
General Principles of Property Valuation for Taxation Purposes. Under Washington
law, all property must be valued at “one hundred percent of . . . true and fair value.”7 True and
fair value is synonymous with fair market value,8 which “is the amount of money a buyer of
property willing but not obligated to buy would pay a seller of property willing but not obligated
to sell.”9 To reach an opinion of fair market value, the appraiser must consider a property’s
highest and best use,10 unless the use is prohibited “under existing zoning or land use planning
ordinances or statutes or other government restrictions.”11 In the course of determining a
property’s value, assessors must allocate the value to the land and the structures, giving care that
the sum of those values does not “exceed the true and fair value of the total property as it
exists.”12
Washington law13 requires that fair market value be determined using the sales
comparison approach, with further consideration of the cost and income capitalization
approaches if there are not sufficient comparable sales available. In the absence of a sufficient
number of comparable sales, or when valuing a complex property, either the cost or income
capitalization approach, or both, “must be the dominant factors in valuation.”14 The assessed
values of other properties do not constitute relevant evidence of the subject property’s market value,
nor does the assessed value of the subject property from a previous or subsequent assessment year.15
A comparison of assessed values is not a recognized appraisal practice, nor is it authorized by RCW
84.40.030(3).
Sales Comparison Approach. In the sales comparison approach,16 an appraiser arrives at a
property’s fair market value by considering sales of the property being appraised or sales of

phrase ‘true and fair value in money’ has been consistently interpreted to mean ‘fair market value’”).
9 WAC 458-07-030(1).
10 WAC 458-07-030(3).
11 RCW 84.40.030(3)(a).

fixtures of whatsoever kind thereon.” RCW 84.40.030(3)(c) “necessarily contemplates the potential adjustment of

King County, 106 Wn. App. 321, 326, 23 P.3d 1090 (2001).
13 RCW 84.40.030(3).

similar properties occurring within the past five years.17 Key factors for determining whether a
sale property and the subject property are “similar” include: (1) location; (2) age, size, construction
quality, and condition of improvements; and (3) special features of the site, such as view or
waterfront.18 The Board places the greatest weight on sales most similar to the subject property
that sold closest to the assessment date.19
Burden of Proof. Under RCW 84.40.0301, an assessor’s original valuation of property is
presumed correct, a presumption that applies solely to the assessor’s valuation, not to any decision
of a county board of equalization.20 To overcome an assessor’s presumption of correctness, and for
an owner or taxpayer to prevail on appeal, the record must contain “clear, cogent and
convincing”21 evidence sufficient to indicate that a value correction is in order. The “clear, cogent,
and convincing” standard requires “proof that is less than ‘beyond a reasonable doubt,’ but more
than a mere ‘preponderance’”; evidence is “clear, cogent, and convincing” if it shows “that the
fact in issue is ‘highly probable.’”22
Authority of the Board of Tax Appeals. To resolve a property valuation appeal, the Board
holds a de novo, or new, hearing and relies on the testimony and evidence presented to the
Board.23 Consistent with RCW 84.40.030(1), the Board may uphold either party’s contended
value or find a different value. Under RCW 84.08.060, however, “the board of tax appeals . . .
shall not raise the valuation of the property to an amount greater than the larger of either the
valuation of the property by the county assessor or the valuation of the property assigned by the
county board of equalization.” Ultimately, the Board makes “such order as in its judgment is just
and proper.”24

occurring closest to the assessment date which require the fewest adjustments for characteristics”). In some
